title: Project structure, packaging and virtual environments
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Put code in `src/mytool/` with tests in `tests/` and metadata in `pyproject.toml`.
A virtual environment gives each project its own interpreter and packages, so one tool upgrading a library does not break another.
A range such as `requests>=2` lets a new release change behaviour overnight.
Declare `[project.scripts] mytool = "mytool.cli:main"` and the installer creates a `mytool` command.
In CI and container builds install from the lock file with hashes where possible, use a slim base image, and copy the lock file before the source so the dependency layer is cached.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A tool that broke after a library release
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A scheduled job failed because a dependency released a breaking version overnight.
An operator runs a command such as: pip list --format=freeze | grep -i requests
The requirements file used a loose range, so the next build picked up a new major release.
The team locked exact versions, committed the lock file and used a scheduled update job that runs the tests before any bump is merged.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Installing into the system Python.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: CLI tools with argparse, click and typer
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A good tool has subcommands such as `mytool backup run` and `mytool backup list`, options with defaults and help text for each.
Return 0 on success and a non zero code on failure so scripts and schedulers can react.
Destructive tools need a `--dry-run` that prints what would change, and often a required `--yes` or a typed confirmation for production.
Provide `--output json` for scripts alongside readable text for people.
`argparse` is enough for most tools.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A cleanup tool that ran against production
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
An engineer meant to test a cleanup in staging, but the default target was production.
An operator runs a command such as: mytool cleanup --older-than 30d
The tool defaulted to production and had no dry run, so the first run was real.
The team made the environment a required argument, added --dry-run as the default behaviour for destructive commands and printed the target in the first line of output.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Defaulting to production.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: API clients: retries, timeouts and pagination
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A request with no timeout can wait forever and hang a scheduled job.
When a call fails with a transient error, wait and try again, doubling the wait each time up to a limit and adding random jitter so many clients do not retry in step.
A `GET` is safe to retry. This keeps the next step safe and easy to check.
APIs return 429 and often a `Retry-After` header.
Large lists arrive in pages. This keeps the next step safe and easy to check.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A report that missed most of the data
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A usage report counted only the first hundred resources because pagination was ignored.
An operator runs a command such as: python report.py --count
The client read one page and ignored the next page token, so the report looked plausible but was wrong.
The team replaced it with a generator that follows tokens until none remain and added a test with a fake API that returns three pages.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: No timeout on requests.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Concurrency: threads, asyncio and processes
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: I/O bound work waits for networks, disks and APIs, so many tasks can overlap.
A `ThreadPoolExecutor` runs a function over many inputs with a fixed number of workers and is the simplest way to parallelise blocking calls such as SSH or HTTP.
`asyncio` runs many tasks on one thread by switching at `await` points.
`ProcessPoolExecutor` uses separate processes and so separate interpreters, which gives real parallelism for CPU bound work.
Unlimited concurrency overloads the target and your own file descriptors.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A health check that opened too many connections
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A script checking 3000 hosts at once exhausted file descriptors and failed halfway.
An operator runs a command such as: ulimit -n
The script started every check at once.
The team added a semaphore of 50 concurrent checks, set a per host timeout and collected failures into a report instead of stopping at the first exception.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Threads for CPU heavy work.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Testing with pytest and mocking infrastructure
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A test is a function whose name starts with `test_` and uses plain `assert`.
`@pytest.mark.parametrize` runs one test with many inputs.
Separate logic from I/O. This keeps the next step safe and easy to check.
Use `tmp_path` for files, `monkeypatch.setenv` for environment variables and pass the current time in as an argument or use a clock function you can replace.
Test decisions: which resources are selected for deletion, how retries behave, how errors are reported.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A cleanup that deleted the wrong resources
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A change to a selection rule removed resources that were still in use, and no test covered it.
An operator runs a command such as: pytest -q
The rule for tagged resources had no test, so the change passed.
The team wrote parametrised cases for tags, ages and missing fields, ran them with a fake client in CI and required them to pass before any change to the selection logic could be merged.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Logic mixed into I/O code.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Cloud and Kubernetes SDKs with safe patterns
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Automation should use short lived credentials from a role or workload identity, not long lived keys in files.
Build the list of targets first, print it and apply filters such as tags and age.
Tag everything automation creates with the owner and the tool.
The official client loads configuration from a kubeconfig or from the service account inside a pod.

Cap how many resources one run may change, require an explicit flag or approval for large changes, check that the account and region are the expected ones, and provide a kill switch such as a feature flag file.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: An automation that tried to delete half the account
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A cleanup script matched far more resources than intended because a tag filter was empty.
An operator runs a command such as: python cleanup.py --dry-run
An empty tag value matched everything.
The run stopped because of the per run limit that the team had added after an earlier near miss.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Long lived keys in scripts.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
